title: Mathlib Imports
content: This proof uses Mathlib's prime number definitions, factorial properties, modular arithmetic, and general tactics. The key external facts are `Nat.exists_prime_and_dvd` (every n >= 2 has a prime factor) and `Nat.dvd_factorial` (primes up to n divide n!).

title: Multiplicativity of Residue 1 (mod 3)
content: The product of two integers each congruent to 1 (mod 3) is also congruent to 1 (mod 3). This is because (Z/3Z)* is a group and 1 is the identity. Proved by direct calculation using `Nat.mul_mod`.

title: Factoring Determines Residue (Strong Induction)
content: The most technical lemma: if all prime factors of n are either 3 or congruent to 1 (mod 3), then n cannot be congruent to 2 (mod 3). Proved by strong induction on n. The base cases handle n = 1 (trivial) and the case where n = p (a single prime factor). The inductive step extracts a prime factor p with p % 3 = 1, divides out to get m = n/p, shows m has the same factor property, and uses m % 3 = 2 (from n = p*m with n % 3 = 2, p % 3 = 1) to apply the inductive hypothesis.

title: The Euclid-Style Construction
content: Given any n, consider N = 3*(n+1)! - 1. This satisfies N = 2 (mod 3) and N >= 2. By has_prime_factor_2_mod_3, N has a prime factor p with p = 2 (mod 3). The key size argument: if p <= n+1 then p | (n+1)! and hence p | 3*(n+1)!, but also p | N, so p | (3*(n+1)! - N) = 1, contradicting p being prime. Therefore p > n.
